Interpolating Discrete Diffusion Models with Controllable Resampling

Marcel Kollovieh Affiliation: School of Computation, Information and Technology, Technical University of Munich Affiliation: Munich Data Science Institute Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning Correspondence to: m.kollovieh@tum.de    Sirine Ayadi Affiliation: School of Computation, Information and Technology, Technical University of Munich Affiliation: Munich Data Science Institute    Stephan Günnemann Affiliation: School of Computation, Information and Technology, Technical University of Munich Affiliation: Munich Data Science Institute Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning
Abstract

Discrete diffusion models form a powerful class of generative models across diverse domains, including text and graphs. However, existing approaches face fundamental limitations. Masked diffusion models suffer from irreversible errors due to early unmasking, while uniform diffusion models, despite enabling self-correction, often yield low-quality samples due to their strong reliance on intermediate latent states. We introduce IDDM, an Interpolating Discrete Diffusion Model, that improves diffusion by reducing dependence on intermediate latent states. Central to IDDM is a controllable resampling mechanism that partially resets probability mass to the marginal distribution, mitigating error accumulation and enabling more effective token corrections. IDDM specifies a generative process whose transitions interpolate between staying at the current state, resampling from a prior, and flipping toward the target state, while enforcing marginal consistency and fully decoupling training from inference. We benchmark our model against state-of-the-art discrete diffusion models across molecular graph generation as well as text generation tasks, demonstrating competitive performance.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Discrete diffusion models (Austin et al., 2021) have emerged as a powerful approach for generating structures across domains such as proteins (Gruver et al., 2023; Nisonoff et al., 2024), DNA sequences (Sarkar et al., 2024), and molecules (Vignac et al., 2022; Campbell et al., 2022), and are starting to catch up with autoregressive models in language generation (Lou et al., 2023; Sahoo et al., 2025; Schiff et al., 2024). As with their continuous counterparts, the core idea is to define Markov transitions that gradually corrupt the data, and then learn a model to denoise it by parametrizing the reverse process. Common forward processes include uniform transitions over the state space or masking, also known as absorbing-state diffusion, in which the state either remains unchanged or transitions to a mask token (Austin et al., 2021; Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024).

While these frameworks work analogously to the continuous case, they introduce considerable limitations. Masked diffusion models, for example, do not support refinement: once a token is unmasked, it remains fixed throughout the entire generation, restricting the model to correct earlier mistakes and leading to error accumulation (Sahoo et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024; Boget, 2025). Uniform transitions, on the other hand, allow flips back to the prior, but they can still suffer from error accumulation (Boget, 2025), and are typically outperformed by absorbing-state diffusion approaches (Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2023).

In this work, we propose Interpolating Discrete Diffusion Model (IDDM), a generative model for discrete data that derives transition probabilities from a different perspective. Instead of defining a Markovian forward transition to reach a terminal distribution, we directly define the reverse, i.e., the generative distribution. To this end, our transitions make use of three different actions: (i) staying in the current state, (ii) transitioning to the goal state, and (iii) resampling from the prior distribution, see Figure 1.

By constraining the marginal distribution to match an interpolation from prior to the data distribution, we obtain a family of posterior transitions. The posteriors interpolate between a fully local update without random flips and a state-independent update that discards the current state, enabling us to trade off preservation of the current knowledge and stochasticity. To demonstrate IDDM’s capability, we evaluate it on molecule generation and language tasks.

Contributions.

Our contributions can be summarized as:

  • •

    Interpolating reverse dynamics. We propose the Interpolating Discrete Diffusion Model (IDDM), a simple discrete diffusion model consisting of three different actions, i.e., stay in the current state, transition to the goal state, resample from the prior.

  • •

    Marginal-consistent posterior family. By enforcing that the marginals adhere to an interpolation between the prior and the data distribution, we derive a family of posterior transitions that trades off preserving the current state against injecting stochasticity.

  • •

    Forward-process interpretation. We show that the resulting transitions correspond, in general, to a non-Markovian forward process.

  • •

    Empirical evaluation. We demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance on well-established benchmarks for molecule generation and language modeling.

2 Discrete Diffusion Models

Notations.

For clarity and ease of presentation, we use 𝐱\mathbf{x} to denote a single discrete random variable taking values in {1,…,K}\{1,\dots,K\}. In sequence modeling, 𝐱\mathbf{x} represents a single token, while in graph modeling, it can represent a single node or a single edge in the graph. We denote the corresponding one-hot encoding by 𝐞𝐱∈ΔK−1\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}\in\Delta^{K-1}, where ΔK−1\Delta^{K-1} is the simplex over KK categories. We denote by Cat⁡(⋅,𝐲)\Cat(\cdot;\mathbf{y}) the categorical distribution with probability vector 𝐲∈ΔK−1\mathbf{y}\in\Delta^{K-1}.

Diffusion models learn a Markov chain that involves a forward process to perturb the data 𝐱∼𝐪0​(𝐱)\mathbf{x}\sim\mathbf{q}_{0}(\mathbf{x}) to increasingly noisy latent variables 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}, for t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], and a trained reverse process. The forward process p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱s)p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s}) is expressed under the Markovian assumption, and the induced marginal for every latent variable 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} can be defined as an interpolation between the clean data and a noisy prior 𝐪1\mathbf{q}_{1} (Sahoo et al., 2024):

p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱)=Cat⁡(𝐱t,(1−αt)​𝐪1+αt​𝐞𝐱),p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x})\;=\;\Cat(\mathbf{x}_{t};(1\;-\;\alpha_{t})\mathbf{q}_{1}\;+\;\alpha_{t}\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}})\;, (1)

where αt∈[0,1]\alpha_{t}\in[0,1] is a strictly decreasing function in tt, and unless stated otherwise, 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} is represented in one-hot form. The parametrized reverse process pθ​(𝐱s∣𝐱t,𝐱),s<tp_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}),s<t is trained to optimize a variational lower bound on the log-likelihood:

log\displaystyle\log\ pθ​(𝐱)≥\displaystyle p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\geq
𝔼p⁡(𝐱t⁡(1),…,𝐱t⁡(T)∣𝐱)​[log⁡pθ​(𝐱,𝐱t⁡(1),…,𝐱t⁡(T))p⁡(𝐱t⁡(1),…,𝐱t⁡(T)∣𝐱)],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p(\mathbf{x}_{t(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t(T)}\mid\mathbf{x})}\left[\log\frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_{t(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t(T)})}{p(\mathbf{x}_{t(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t(T)}\mid\mathbf{x})}\right], (2)

where t⁡(i)=i/Tt(i)=i/T, TT is the number of diffusion steps, and the reverse Markov process

pθ(𝐱,𝐱t⁡(1:T))=\displaystyle p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_{t(1:T)})=
p⁡(𝐱t⁡(T))​∏i=2Tpθ​(𝐱t⁡(i−1)∣𝐱t⁡(i))​pθ​(𝐱∣𝐱t⁡(1)),\displaystyle\qquad p(\mathbf{x}_{t(T)})\,\prod_{i=2}^{T}p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t(i-1)}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t(i)})\,p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t(1)}), (3)

gradually denoises the latent states towards the data distribution. There exist two popular variants for interpolating discrete diffusion models: uniform diffusion models with a stationary distribution 𝐪1=𝟏/K\mathbf{q}_{1}=\bm{1}/K, where 𝟏\bm{1} is a K−K-dimensional column vector of all ones, and masked diffusion models, also known as absorbing state diffusion, where the space is augmented with a special mask token, and the prior distribution is set to 𝐪1=𝐦\mathbf{q}_{1}=\mathbf{m}. Marginal distributions over node and edge attributes as noise have proven to be more suitable for graph generation.

Standard discrete diffusion models tightly couple the reverse process to a fixed forward corruption mechanism. The forward process is defined as a Markov chain p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱s)p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s}), and the reverse transitions can be determined via Bayes’ rule:

p⁡(𝐱s∣𝐱t,𝐱)=p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱s)​p​(𝐱s∣𝐱)p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱),p(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x})=\frac{p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s})p(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x})}\;,

where p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱s)=p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱s,𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s})=p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s},\mathbf{x}) follows from the Markov property. As a result, the reverse dynamics are largely determined once the forward kernel and the noise schedule are fixed. This can limit the extent to which reverse updates can be modified independently of the noising process and, consequently, can negatively impact the sample quality. For example, in absorbing-state diffusion, once a token is unmasked, it remains fixed for the remainder of the generative process. This can lead to systematic error accumulation as early mistakes cannot be recovered. Uniform diffusion models, on the other hand, inherently enable self-correction since the latent states 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} can be continuously updated throughout the reverse process. However, this mechanism can also introduce errors, as correctly predicted tokens can be randomly resampled from the uniform prior.

3 Methodology

In this section, we propose Interpolating Discrete Diffusion Model (IDDM), a simple generative model for discrete data that enables controlled resampling during inference and improves token correction. We provide an overview of IDDM in Figure 2. Our goal is to learn the target distribution 𝐪0\mathbf{q}_{0}. Similar to diffusion models, we define a sequence of latent variables 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} that interpolate between the data at t=0t=0 and a prior distribution at t=1t=1. However, unlike diffusion models, we do not explicitly define forward, i.e., noising process p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱s,𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s},\mathbf{x}), for s<ts<t. Instead, we define the reverse-time generative process directly.

We start by defining our posterior transition probability with three actions: (i) stay at the current state, (ii) flip to the goal state 𝐞𝐱\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}, or (iii) resample from the prior 𝐪1\mathbf{q}_{1}. More specifically:

p⁡(𝐱s∣𝐱t,𝐱)\displaystyle p(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}) =Cat⁡(wstay​𝐱t+wprior​𝐪1+wflip​𝐞𝐱),\displaystyle=\Cat\Big(w_{\mathrm{stay}}\mathbf{x}_{t}+w_{\mathrm{prior}}\mathbf{q}_{1}+w_{\mathrm{flip}}\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}\Big), (4)

with wstay,wflip,wprior≥0w_{\mathrm{stay}},w_{\mathrm{flip}},w_{\mathrm{prior}}\geq 0 and wstay+wflip+wprior=1w_{\mathrm{stay}}+w_{\mathrm{flip}}+w_{\mathrm{prior}}=1.

Marginal distribution.

We constrain the marginal distribution to interpolate between the prior distribution and the goal state:

p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱)\displaystyle p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}) =Cat⁡(𝐱t,(1−γt)​𝐪1+γt​𝐞𝐱),\displaystyle=\Cat\!\Big(\mathbf{x}_{t};\,(1-\gamma_{t})\mathbf{q}_{1}+\gamma_{t}\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}\Big), (5)

with γt∈[0,1]\gamma_{t}\in[0,1], γ1=0\gamma_{1}=0 and γ0=1\gamma_{0}=1. This choice enables direct sampling of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} at arbitrary tt without simulating intermediate states.

Parametrization of transition weights.

To enforce p⁡(𝐱s∣𝐱)=Cat⁡((1−γs)​𝐪1+γs​𝐞𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x})=\Cat((1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}+\gamma_{s}\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}) for all s<ts<t, our weights must satisfy the following constraints:

(1)​wstay​(1−γt)+wprior=1−γs,and\displaystyle(1)\,w_{\mathrm{stay}}(1-\gamma_{t})+w_{\mathrm{prior}}=1-\gamma_{s},\quad\text{and}
(2)​wstay​γt+wflip=γs.\displaystyle(2)\,w_{\mathrm{stay}}\gamma_{t}+w_{\mathrm{flip}}=\gamma_{s}. (6)

We use this to introduce a forgetting parameter λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] that interpolates between a purely local update (λ=0\lambda=0) and a global reset to the marginal at time ss (λ=1\lambda=1).

∑𝐱tpλ​(𝐱s∣𝐱t,𝐱)​p​(𝐱t∣𝐱)=p⁡(𝐱s∣𝐱),for all ​s<t,\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x})\,p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x})=p(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}),\quad\text{for all }s<t, (12)

Special cases.

The parameter λ\lambda acts as a forget mechanism controlling how much probability mass is taken from the current state 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}, and how much is resampled independently from the marginal. Figure 3 visualizes the transition distributions p⁡(𝐱s∣𝐱t,𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}) for increasing values of λ\lambda. At λ=0\lambda=0, our model reduces to two choices, i.e., either remain in the current state, or flip to the data token. More specifically,

p0​(𝐱s∣𝐱t,𝐱)=Cat⁡(𝐱s,γs|t​𝐱t+(1−γs|t)​𝐞x).\displaystyle p_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x})=\Cat\!\Big(\mathbf{x}_{s};\gamma_{s\mid t}\,\mathbf{x}_{t}+\Big(1-\gamma_{s\mid t}\Big)\mathbf{e}_{x}\Big). (13)

This dynamics defines an absorbing diffusion process directed toward the data token 𝐞𝐱\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}. In particular, when 𝐱t=𝐞𝐱\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}, the transition distribution collapses to p0​(𝐱s∣𝐱t=𝐞𝐱,𝐱)=Cat⁡(𝐱s;𝐞𝐱)p_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{x})=\Cat\!\big(\mathbf{x}_{s};\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}\big) indicating that 𝐞𝐱\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}} is absorbing and every other state 𝐱t≠𝐞𝐱\mathbf{x}_{t}\neq\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}} remains non-absorbing, with a nonzero probability of transitioning to 𝐞𝐱\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}. This behavior is reflected in Figure 3, where probability mass is concentrated along the diagonal and the column corresponding to the data point 𝐱\mathbf{x}. For λ=1\lambda=1, the posterior reduces to:

p1​(𝐱s∣𝐱t,𝐱)\displaystyle p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}) =Cat⁡(𝐱s,(1−γs)​𝐪1+γs​𝐞x)\displaystyle=\Cat\!\Big(\mathbf{x}_{s};(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}+\gamma_{s}\mathbf{e}_{x}\Big) (14)
=p⁡(𝐱s∣𝐱).\displaystyle=p(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}).

In this case, the latent variables 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} and 𝐱s\mathbf{x}_{s} are conditionally independent given 𝐱\mathbf{x}, i.e., the state 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} is entirely discarded, and the transitions reset to the marginal distribution. This is illustrated in Figure 3 where all rows collapse to the same distribution, reflecting complete forgetting of the current state 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}.

Remark on the forward process.

Our approach does not require instantiating a Markovian noising process p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱s)p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s}), for s<ts<t, following standard diffusion methods. Instead, we directly sample the noisy latents from the marginal distribution in equation 5. For completeness, however, we derive the underlying forward transition step of IDDM via Bayes’ rule, pλ​(𝐱t∣𝐱s,𝐱)∝pλ​(𝐱s∣𝐱t,𝐱)​p​(𝐱t∣𝐱).p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s},\mathbf{x})\propto p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}). This induces a non-Markovian forward kernel of the form:

pλ​(𝐱t∣𝐱s,𝐱)=Cat⁡(𝐱t,α𝐱s​𝐦t+(1−α𝐱s)​𝐱s),p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s},\mathbf{x})=\Cat\Big(\mathbf{x}_{t};\alpha_{\mathbf{x}_{s}}\mathbf{m}_{t}+(1-\alpha_{\mathbf{x}_{s}})\mathbf{x}_{s}\Big)\;, (15)

where 𝐦t=p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱)\mathbf{m}_{t}=p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}) and α𝐱s∈[0,1]\alpha_{\mathbf{x}_{s}}\in[0,1] is a state-dependent resampling probability. This transition admits a simple interpretation: with probability α𝐱s\alpha_{\mathbf{x}_{s}}, the latent 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} is resampled from the marginal distribution, otherwise the state retains the previous state 𝐱s\mathbf{x}_{s} with probability 1−α𝐱s1-\alpha_{\mathbf{x}_{s}}. We provide a full derivation in Appendix B. Crucially, our marginal is independent of the resampling scheduler λ\lambda, allowing decoupled training and sampling.

3.1 Generative Distribution and optimization

As the true sample 𝐱\mathbf{x} is not known during inference, we train a neural network as a surrogate. We define the generative distribution as follows:

pλθ​(𝐱s∣𝐱t)\displaystyle p_{\lambda}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) =Cat⁡(𝐱s;(1−λ)​[γs|t​𝐱t+(1−γs|t)​𝐱θ]CLOSE\displaystyle=\Cat\!\Big(\mathbf{x}_{s};(1-\lambda)\big[\gamma_{s\mid t}\,\mathbf{x}_{t}+(1-\gamma_{s\mid t})\mathbf{x}_{\theta}\big]
OPEN+λ⁡[(1−γs)​𝐪1+γs​𝐱θ]),\displaystyle\qquad+\lambda\big[(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}+\gamma_{s}\mathbf{x}_{\theta}\big]\Big), (16)

where 𝐱θ≔fθ​(𝐱t,t)\mathbf{x}_{\theta}\coloneqq f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) is a neural network prediction. As with standard diffusion models, we aim to optimize the log-likelihood log⁡pθ​(𝐱)\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}). However, due to the intractability of the marginalization, we derive the evidence lower bound (ELBO):

log⁡pλθ​(𝐱)≥\displaystyle\log p_{\lambda}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\geq

=𝔼pλ​(𝐱t⁡(1)∣𝐱)​[log⁡pλθ​(𝐱∣𝐱t⁡(1))]\displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t(1)}\mid\mathbf{x})}\!\left[\log p_{\lambda}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t(1)})\right]
−∑i=2T𝔼pλ​(𝐱t⁡(i)∣𝐱)[ℒdiff(i)]\displaystyle\qquad-\;\sum_{i=2}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t(i)}\mid\mathbf{x})}\!\left[\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}^{(i)}\right]\;
−𝔼𝐪0​(𝐱)[KL(p(𝐱t⁡(T)∣𝐱)∥p(𝐱t⁡(T)))],\displaystyle\qquad-\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{q}_{0}(\mathbf{x})}\bigg[\mathrm{KL}\!\Big(p(\mathbf{x}_{t(T)}\mid\mathbf{x})\,\big\|\,p(\mathbf{x}_{t(T)})\Big)\bigg]\;, (17)

where

ℒdiff(i)=KL(pλ(𝐱t⁡(i−1)∣𝐱t⁡(i),𝐱)∥pλθ(𝐱t⁡(i−1)∣𝐱t⁡(i))).\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}^{(i)}=\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t(i-1)}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t(i)},\mathbf{x})\,\big\lVert\,p_{\lambda}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t(i-1)}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t(i)})\right).

The ELBO is maximized when the KL divergences between the two distributions are minimized, i.e., when the neural network fθf_{\theta} predicts 𝐞𝐱\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}. As the ELBOs share the same optimum across all λ\lambda when the model perfectly predicts 𝐱\mathbf{x}, we only need to train one model, allowing us to change λ\lambda only during inference. We provide the training and sampling algorithms of IDDM in Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2, respectively.

Expected total number of state transitions.

In the following, we analyze the expected number of state transitions induced by IDDM, i.e., 𝐱t⁡(k−1)≠𝐱t⁡(k)\mathbf{x}_{t(k-1)}\neq\mathbf{x}_{t(k)}, for k∈{1,⋯,T}k\in\{1,\cdots,T\}, along a generation trajectory of TT steps. Let

Ck=𝟏[𝐱t⁡(k−1)≠𝐱t⁡(k)]C_{k}=\mathbf{1}\Big[\mathbf{x}_{t(k-1)}\neq\mathbf{x}_{t(k)}\Big]

denote the indicator of a state change at step kk. The expected total number of transitions is then given by:

𝔼λ​[NT]=𝔼λ​[∑k=1TCk]=∑k=1T𝔼λ​[pλ​(Ck=1∣𝐱t⁡(k))].\mathbb{E}_{\lambda}\big[N_{T}\big]=\mathbb{E}_{\lambda}\Bigg[\sum_{k=1}^{T}C_{k}\Bigg]=\sum_{k=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{\lambda}\Big[p_{\lambda}(C_{k}=1\mid\mathbf{x}_{t(k)})\Big].

In Appendix C, we show that this expectation admits the form 𝔼λ​[NT]=A​λ+B\mathbb{E}_{\lambda}\big[N_{T}\big]=A\lambda+B, where A,B≥0A,B\geq 0. This implies that the expected number of state transitions grows linearly with the resampling coefficient λ\lambda. In practice, however, the model fθ​(𝐱t,t)f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) does not perfectly preserve the marginal, therefore the distribution of 𝐱t⁡(k)\mathbf{x}_{t(k)} can drift with λ\lambda. We investigate this effect in Section 4.4.

Extension to graphs and sequences.

So far, we have considered a single-token data point 𝐱\mathbf{x}. IDDM can be readily applied to arbitrary discrete domains and accommodates arbitrary prior distributions. In this paper, we apply IDDM to both graph and sequence generation tasks. We represent a graph G=(𝐗,𝐄)G=(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{E}) with NN nodes, where 𝐗∈ℝN×K1\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times K_{1}} is a matrix of one-hot encoded representations of each node 𝐱i∈{0,1}K1\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{K_{1}}, and 𝐄∈ℝN×N×K2\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times K_{2}} groups the one-hot encoding of each edge 𝐞i​j∈{0,1}K2\mathbf{e}_{ij}\in\{0,1\}^{K_{2}}. Here, K1K_{1} and K2K_{2} denote the number of possible node and edge attributes, respectively. We adopt marginal prior distributions over nodes and edges, as they have proved effective in prior graph diffusion approaches (Vignac et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2024). For sequence generation, a sequence is represented as 𝐒∈ℝL×K\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times K}, where LL is the sequence length and KK is the vocabulary size. In this work, we mainly focus on uniform priors, as we find that they consistently yield lower performance than absorbing-state diffusion models in language modeling (Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2023).

4 Experiments

In this section, we discuss our empirical evaluation across various benchmarks. Our primary goal is to compare our generative model to previous discrete diffusion approaches and investigate the effect of random flips to the prior distribution. We benchmark our model on two tasks: graph generation in Section 4.1 and text generation in Section 4.2. Additional details on the datasets, model architectures, training, and evaluation metrics are provided in Appendix D.

4.1 Graph Generation

Experimental setup.

For graph generation, we parametrize our neural network with the graph transformer of Vignac et al. (2022), using Relative Random Walk Probabilities (RRWP) (Ma et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2024) to encode structural properties. The network predicts and generates node and edge labels (see  Section 3.1). We provide additional details and hyperparameters in Section D.3.

Small molecules.

We evaluate our model on the QM9 dataset (Wu et al., 2018) (without hydrogen). The results and baselines are reported in Table 1.

Overall, IDDM faithfully learns the data distribution, achieving a validity of 99.3%, matching the training distribution, and achieves state-of-the-art FCD results with λ=0\lambda=0 and a time distortion scheduler with ρ=4\rho=4, see Section 4.3 for more details.

Large molecules.

In addition to QM9, we evaluate IDDM on the two established benchmarks GuacaMol (Brown et al., 2019) and MOSES (Polykovskiy et al., 2020). We follow the standard data splits and provide our experimental results in Table 2. We observe that our model excels in FCD, SNN, and Filters while maintaining a high validity. Notably, our model with reduced steps (10% of steps) outperforms DeFoG with reduced steps across most metrics. Also, the full-step model achieves a higher validity than DeFoG. For these results, we used ρ=4\rho=4 for both datasets, and λ=0.4\lambda=0.4 for MOSES and λ=0.2\lambda=0.2 for GuacaMol.

4.2 Text Generation

Experimental setting.

We train IDDM on two datasets: the One Billion Words Dataset (LM1B) (Chelba et al., 2013) and OpenWebText (OWT) (Gokaslan & Cohen, 2019). We use the same data splits as Wang et al. (2025) and follow their tokenization and model configurations. For evaluation, we assess language modeling performance using likelihood-based metrics and report perplexity on the test split. To evaluate the quality of generated sequences, we compute generative perplexity (Gen PPL) using GPT-2 Large, and measure sentence entropy to assess output diversity.

Likelihood evaluation.

We compute the perplexity on LM1B and report results in Table 3. Our primary baselines are uniform discrete diffusion models, including D3PM (uniform) (Austin et al., 2021) and SEDD (uniform) (Lou et al., 2023). We further include an autoregressive baseline, as well as absorbing-state diffusion models such as D3PM (absorb) and MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024). Compared to prior diffusion baselines, IDDM consistently improves performance within the uniform diffusion family, with SEDD (Uniform) (Lou et al., 2023) achieving the lowest perplexity. As shown in Figure 4, we analyze perplexity scaling with respect to the number of diffusion steps. Using a fixed resampling parameter λ=0.2\lambda=0.2, IDDM attains strong performance with as few as 16 steps and outperforms both D3PM Uniform and D3PM Absorb by a substantial margin. Additional results with different resampling parameters are presented in Figure 10.

Sample quality.

We assess the generation capability of IDDM when training on OpenWebText. In Table 4, we report the generative perplexity and the entropy for generation steps in {1024,512,256}\{1024,512,256\}. We use λ=0.2\lambda=0.2 for sampling. IDDM achieves comparable generative perplexity to SEDD (uniform) (Lou et al., 2023), while providing improved diversity.

4.3 Time distortion

Following previous works, we distort time steps during sampling (Karras et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2024). Instead of uniformly spacing the time steps, we allocate more steps to later stages of generation, i.e., closer to the final sample. More specifically, we use a similar scheduler as (Karras et al., 2022):

t​(i)′=t​(i)ρ,\displaystyle t(i)^{\prime}=t(i)^{\rho},

with ρ>1\rho>1. We analyze the effect of ρ\rho in Figure 5 and report the FCD and validity for MOSES across different settings. Increasing ρ\rho above 11 yields a substantial improvement while stagnating from ρ=2\rho=2. We provide additional ablations in Appendix E.

4.4 Effect of λ\lambda

Intuitively, increasing λ\lambda introduces more transitions, i.e., 𝐱t≠𝐱s\mathbf{x}_{t}\neq\mathbf{x}_{s}, during generation as the weights wflipw_{\mathrm{flip}} and wpriorw_{\mathrm{prior}} increase. In the extreme case λ=0\lambda=0, the transition in equation 4 reduces to a purely local update and will have at most one transition to the goal state. In practice, however, our trained neural network is not guaranteed to consistently predict the same class, which can lead to additional transitions.

To quantify this effect, we measure the average number of state transitions over 5050 sampling steps on QM9, for the nodes and edges. We show the results in Figure 6.

We observe that the number of transitions increases linearly with λ\lambda, starting close to 0. Note that the average number of transitions for λ=0\lambda=0 is well below 1, as we have a highly imbalanced class distribution and our sampling algorithm starts from the marginal distribution. We show its empirical effect on performance in Figure 5.

5 Related Work

Discrete Diffusion models.

Diffusion models were first introduced for continuous data  (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015), and have demonstrated strong generative performance across a range of domains, including images (Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021; Ho et al., 2020), audio (Kong et al., 2020), and video (Ho et al., 2022). The extension of diffusion models to discrete data was first explored by Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015), which adopted a binomial diffusion process for binary data. Building on this, Hoogeboom et al. (2021) generalized the framework to categorical random variables using transition matrices with uniform corruption probabilities. Austin et al. (2021) propose more structured categorical corruption processes for certain data types, such as absorbing-state diffusion for sequences, and discretized Gaussian kernels for ordinal data.

Recent works (Sahoo et al., 2024) examine a special case of the corruption process in Austin et al. (2021), reformulating it as an interpolation between clean data and a prior distribution. In particular, Sahoo et al. (2024) focus on masked diffusion models, and derive a simplified expression of the ELBO, showing that it corresponds to a weighted average of cross-entropy losses. Schiff et al. (2024) extend this to uniform noise models and provide a continuous-time NELBO leading to performance gains. Sahoo et al. (2025) propose a hybrid model that combines a discrete diffusion process with a Gaussian diffusion process defined directly over one-hot token representations rather than continuous embeddings. Alternative perspectives on discrete diffusion leverage continuous-time Markov chains (CTMC) (Campbell et al., 2022; Campbell et al., 2024) or concrete score matching (Lou et al., 2023).

Graph generation.

Graph generation approaches can be categorized into two classes: autoregressive approaches, which generate nodes and edges sequentially, and one-shot approaches, which rely on diffusion-based methods. Diffusion models leverage the order-agnostic nature of denoising processes to maintain permutation equivariance, and many state-of-the-art approaches further incorporate marginal distributions over node and edge attributes as priors (Vignac et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2024). Recent advances in graph generation have demonstrated that both discrete diffusion models, implemented in either discrete-time settings (Vignac et al., 2022) or continuous-time formulations (Xu et al., 2024), as well as discrete flow-matching approaches (Qin et al., 2024), achieve strong performance in different domains, including molecular and synthetic graph generation. Boget (2025) propose a diffusion model for graphs by assuming that the intermediate noisy states only depend on the clean data, thereby removing the dependence on partially denoised states. This is closely related to IDDM’s extreme case where the resampling coefficient is equal to 1.

Text generation.

For language modeling, autoregressive transformers (Radford et al., 2019; Vaswani et al., 2017) have achieved impressive results. However, their sequential token sampling leads to slow inference and limited controllability. To address this, various works explore discrete diffusion models for language generation. In particular, absorbing-state diffusion models (Shi et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024) have demonstrated strong empirical results; however, they suffer from a key limitation: once a token is unmasked, it cannot be revised, which can cause error accumulation and degrade sample quality. Several predictor-corrector samplers have been proposed (Campbell et al., 2022; Gat et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025) to mitigate this issue, but at the cost of increased computation. In contrast, uniform diffusion models (Austin et al., 2021; Schiff et al., 2024) naturally exhibit a self-correcting property absent in autoregressive and masked diffusion approaches. However, they do not achieve state-of-the-art performance. We note that our IDDM approach naturally enables resampling from arbitrary priors, thereby allowing refinement of tokens for both absorbing-state and uniform diffusion.

6 Discussion

Limitations.

We evaluate our model on graph and text generation. However, our proposed framework applies directly to any other discrete domain, including protein generation (Campbell et al., 2024) and DNA sequences (Stark et al., 2024). Further, our experiments are limited to uniform and marginal priors. Our generative model, however, readily extends to masking-based priors, thereby enabling iterative token refinement.

Future work.

Beyond extending to different domains and prior distributions, future work could investigate the use of guidance and other conditioning techniques. Finally, it would be promising to explore alternative training techniques based on variance reduction or distillation  (Sahoo et al., 2025).

7 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced a discrete diffusion model whose reverse process is expressed by three actions: (i) staying in the current state, (ii) transitioning to the goal state, and (iii) resampling from the prior distribution. By defining a marginal distribution, we derive a family of posteriors that interpolates between a local and a state-independent update, enabling us to directly control the transition frequency, while only training a single model. Further, we show that our reverse process cannot be recovered from a standard Markov noising process, as it corresponds to a non-Markovian forward process. Finally, we demonstrate that IDDM achieves competitive performance on graph and language generation tasks.

Broader Impact

In this work, we propose a generative model for discrete data and apply it to molecule and text generation. As discrete generative models can be applied in various fields, we see potential positive and negative societal impacts. Generative modeling can accelerate scientific discovery and enhance natural language generation capabilities. However, there are potential societal consequences, specifically those related to the generation of harmful text or designing unsafe drugs.

=Cat(𝐱s;𝔼𝐱t∼p(⋅∣𝐱)[wstay𝐱t+wprior𝐪1+wflip𝐞x])\displaystyle=\Cat\Big(\mathbf{x}_{s};\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}\sim p(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x})}[w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{x}_{t}+w_{\text{prior}}\mathbf{q}_{1}+w_{\text{flip}}\mathbf{e}_{x}]\Big)
=Cat⁡(𝐱s,wstay​𝐦t+wprior​𝐪1+wflip​𝐞x)\displaystyle=\Cat\Big(\mathbf{x}_{s};w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{m}_{t}+w_{\text{prior}}\mathbf{q}_{1}+w_{\text{flip}}\mathbf{e}_{x}\Big) (24)

Now we simplify the expressions using the coefficients in equation 19 and equation 21:

wstay​𝐦t\displaystyle w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{m}_{t} =(1−λ)​γs|t​((1−γt)​𝐪1+γt​𝐞x)\displaystyle=(1-\lambda)\,\gamma_{s\mid t}\bigl((1-\gamma_{t})\mathbf{q}_{1}+\gamma_{t}\mathbf{e}_{x}\bigr)
=(1−λ)​1−γs1−γt​(1−γt)​𝐪1+(1−λ)​γs|t​γt​𝐞x\displaystyle=(1-\lambda)\frac{1-\gamma_{s}}{1-\gamma_{t}}(1-\gamma_{t})\mathbf{q}_{1}+(1-\lambda)\gamma_{s\mid t}\gamma_{t}\mathbf{e}_{x}
=(1−λ)​(1−γs)​𝐪1+(1−λ)​γs|t​γt​𝐞x\displaystyle=(1-\lambda)(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}+(1-\lambda)\gamma_{s\mid t}\gamma_{t}\mathbf{e}_{x} (25)
wflip​𝐞x\displaystyle w_{\text{flip}}\mathbf{e}_{x} =((1−λ)​(1−γs|t)+λ​γs)​𝐞x\displaystyle=\bigl((1-\lambda)(1-\gamma_{s\mid t})+\lambda\gamma_{s}\bigr)\mathbf{e}_{x}
=(1−λ)​(1−γs|t)​𝐞x+λ​γs​𝐞x\displaystyle=(1-\lambda)(1-\gamma_{s\mid t})\mathbf{e}_{x}+\lambda\gamma_{s}\mathbf{e}_{x} (26)

Substituting equation 25 and equation 26 into equation 24 yields:

p⁡(𝐱s∣𝐱)\displaystyle p(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}) =Cat⁡(𝐱s,wstay​𝐦t+wprior​𝐪1+wflip​𝐞x)\displaystyle=\Cat\Big(\mathbf{x}_{s};w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{m}_{t}+w_{\text{prior}}\mathbf{q}_{1}+w_{\text{flip}}\mathbf{e}_{x}\Big)

=Cat⁡(𝐱s,(1−γs)​𝐪1+((1−λ)​(1−γs|t​(1−γt))+λ​γs)​𝐞𝐱)\displaystyle=\Cat\Big(\mathbf{x}_{s};(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}+\big((1-\lambda)(1-\gamma_{s\mid t}(1-\gamma_{t}))+\lambda\gamma_{s}\big)\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}\Big)
=Cat⁡(𝐱s,(1−γs)​𝐪1+((1−λ)​(1−1−γs1−γt​(1−γt))+λ​γs)​𝐞𝐱)\displaystyle=\Cat\Big(\mathbf{x}_{s};(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}+\big((1-\lambda)(1-\frac{1-\gamma_{s}}{1-\gamma_{t}}(1-\gamma_{t}))+\lambda\gamma_{s}\big)\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}\Big)

This completes the induction. ∎

Appendix B Derivation of the forward transition pλ​(𝐱t∣𝐱s,𝐱)p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s},\mathbf{x})

In the following, we derive the forward transition step pλ​(𝐱t∣𝐱s,𝐱)p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s},\mathbf{x}). Recall our reverse process defined for λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]:

pλ​(𝐱s∣𝐱t,𝐱)\displaystyle p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}) =Cat⁡(𝐱s;(1−λ)​γs|t​𝐱t+λ⁡(1−γs)​𝐪1CLOSE\displaystyle=\Cat\!\Big(\mathbf{x}_{s};(1-\lambda)\gamma_{s\mid t}\,\mathbf{x}_{t}+\lambda(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1} (27)
OPEN+(1−((1−λ)​γs|t+λ⁡(1−γs)))​𝐞x)\displaystyle+\Big(1-\big((1-\lambda)\gamma_{s\mid t}+\lambda(1-\gamma_{s})\big)\Big)\mathbf{e}_{x}\Big) (28)
=Cat⁡(𝐱s,wstay​𝐱t+wprior​𝐪1+wflip​𝐞𝐱)\displaystyle=\Cat\!\Big(\mathbf{x}_{s};w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{x}_{t}+w_{\text{prior}}\mathbf{q}_{1}+w_{\text{flip}}\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}}\Big) (29)

Let 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} and 𝐞𝐱\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}} be single tokens. We write the categorical parameters in scalar form. The reverse kernel implies that, for any i,j∈{1,…​K}i,j\in\{1,\dots K\},

pλ(𝐱s=i∣𝐱t=j,𝐞𝐱)=wstay𝟏[i=j]+wprior𝐪1(i)+wflip𝟏[i=𝐱].p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{s}=i\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=j,\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}})=w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{1}[i=j]+w_{\text{prior}}\mathbf{q}_{1}(i)+w_{\text{flip}}\mathbf{1}[i=\mathbf{x}].

Let 𝐦t​(j)=p⁡(𝐱t=j∣𝐱)\mathbf{m}_{t}(j)=p(\mathbf{x}_{t}=j\mid\mathbf{x}), where 𝐦t(⋅)=(1−γt)𝐪1(⋅)+γt𝟏[.=𝐱]\mathbf{m}_{t}(\cdot)=(1-\gamma_{t})\mathbf{q}_{1}(\cdot)+\gamma_{t}\mathbf{1}[.=\mathbf{x}].

We first derive the unnormalized forward probabilities: We fix 𝐱s=i\mathbf{x}_{s}=i. Then, for each jj, we have:

pλ​(𝐱t=j∣𝐱s=i,𝐱)\displaystyle p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t}=j\mid\mathbf{x}_{s}=i,\mathbf{x}) ∝pλ​(𝐱s=i∣𝐱t=j,𝐱)​p​(𝐱t=j∣𝐱)\displaystyle\propto p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{s}=i\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=j,\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x}_{t}=j\mid\mathbf{x}) (30)
∝(wstay𝟏[i=j]+wprior𝐪1(i)+wflip𝟏[i=𝐱])𝐦t(j)\displaystyle\propto\big(w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{1}[i=j]+w_{\text{prior}}\mathbf{q}_{1}(i)+w_{\text{flip}}\mathbf{1}[i=\mathbf{x}]\big)\mathbf{m}_{t}(j) (31)
∝(wstay𝟏[i=j]+Di)𝐦t(j),\displaystyle\propto\big(w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{1}[i=j]+D_{i}\big)\mathbf{m}_{t}(j), (32)

where Di=wprior𝐪1(i)+wflip𝟏[i=𝐱]D_{i}=w_{\text{prior}}\mathbf{q}_{1}(i)+w_{\text{flip}}\mathbf{1}[i=\mathbf{x}].

The normalizing constant is p⁡(𝐱s=i∣𝐱)=𝐦s​(i)p(\mathbf{x}_{s}=i\mid\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{m}_{s}(i). We can also derive it as follows:

p⁡(𝐱s=i∣𝐱)\displaystyle p(\mathbf{x}_{s}=i\mid\mathbf{x}) =∑j′pλ​(𝐱s=i∣𝐱t=j′,𝐱)​p​(𝐱t=j′∣𝐱)\displaystyle=\sum_{j^{\prime}}p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{s}=i\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=j^{\prime},\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x}_{t}=j^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{x}) (33)
=∑j′(wstay𝟏[i=j′]+Di)𝐦t(j′)\displaystyle=\sum_{j^{\prime}}(w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{1}[i=j^{\prime}]+D_{i})\mathbf{m}_{t}(j^{\prime}) (34)
=wstay​𝐦t​(i)+Di​∑j′𝐦t​(j′)\displaystyle=w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{m}_{t}(i)+D_{i}\sum_{j^{\prime}}\mathbf{m}_{t}(j^{\prime}) (35)
=wstay​𝐦t​(i)+Di,\displaystyle=w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{m}_{t}(i)+D_{i}\;, (36)

since ∑j′𝐦t​(j′)=1\sum_{j^{\prime}}\mathbf{m}_{t}(j^{\prime})=1. The normalized forward transition of equation 32 is:

pλ​(𝐱t=j∣𝐱s=i,𝐱)=(wstay𝟏[i=j]+Di)𝐦t(j)𝐦s​(i).p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t}=j\mid\mathbf{x}_{s}=i,\mathbf{x})=\frac{\big(w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{1}[i=j]+D_{i}\big)\mathbf{m}_{t}(j)}{\mathbf{m}_{s}(i)}. (37)

If i=ji=j, then:

pλ​(𝐱t=i∣𝐱s=i,𝐱)=(wstay+Di)​𝐦t​(i)𝐦s​(i).p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t}=i\mid\mathbf{x}_{s}=i,\mathbf{x})=\frac{(w_{\text{stay}}+D_{i})\mathbf{m}_{t}(i)}{\mathbf{m}_{s}(i)}.

For i≠ji\neq j:

pλ​(𝐱t=j∣𝐱s=i,𝐱)=Di​𝐦t​(j)𝐦s​(i).p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t}=j\mid\mathbf{x}_{s}=i,\mathbf{x})=\frac{D_{i}\mathbf{m}_{t}(j)}{\mathbf{m}_{s}(i)}.

To further simplify equation 37, we define the coefficient:

αi=Di𝐦s​(i)=Diwstay​𝐦t​(i)+Di∈[0,1].\alpha_{i}=\frac{D_{i}}{\mathbf{m}_{s}(i)}=\frac{D_{i}}{w_{\text{stay}}\mathbf{m}_{t}(i)+D_{i}}\in[0,1]\;. (38)

Then, we can rewrite the distribution over 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} as a mixture:

pλ(𝐱t=j∣𝐱s=i,𝐱)=αi𝐦t(j)+(1−αi)𝟏[j=i].p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t}=j\mid\mathbf{x}_{s}=i,\mathbf{x})=\alpha_{i}\mathbf{m}_{t}(j)+(1-\alpha_{i})\mathbf{1}[j=i]\;. (39)

The final forward transition can be simplified to:

pλ​(𝐱t∣𝐱s,𝐱)=Cat⁡(𝐱t,α𝐱s​𝐦t+(1−α𝐱s)​𝐞𝐱s),p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{s},\mathbf{x})=\Cat(\mathbf{x}_{t};\alpha_{\mathbf{x}_{s}}\mathbf{m}_{t}+(1-\alpha_{\mathbf{x}_{s}})\mathbf{e}_{\mathbf{x}_{s}})\;, (40)

which means that in the forward transition, 𝐱t=𝐱s\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{x}_{s} with probability (1−α𝐱s)(1-\alpha_{\mathbf{x}_{s}}), otherwise we sample from the marginal 𝐱t∼𝐦t=p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱)\mathbf{x}_{t}\sim\mathbf{m}_{t}=p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}). The underlying forward process of IDDM is therefore non-Markovian as it requires access to the clean state 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

Instantiating the forward transitions for the special cases.
For λ=0\lambda=0:

The coefficients in the reverse process are simplified to:

wstay=γs|t,wprior=0,and ​wflip=1−γs|t.w_{\text{stay}}=\gamma_{s\mid t},\quad w_{\text{prior}}=0,\quad\text{and }w_{\text{flip}}=1-\gamma_{s\mid t}.

For λ=1\lambda=1:

The coefficients of the generative process are

wstay=0,wprior=(1−γs),and ​wflip=γsw_{\text{stay}}=0,\quad w_{\text{prior}}=(1-\gamma_{s}),\quad\text{and }w_{\text{flip}}=\gamma_{s}

. Therefore, the Bayes expression in equation 37 collapses to:

p1​(𝐱t=j∣𝐱s=i,𝐱)=Di​𝐦t​(j)Di=𝐦t​(j).p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{t}=j\mid\mathbf{x}_{s}=i,\mathbf{x})=\frac{D_{i}\mathbf{m}_{t}(j)}{D_{i}}=\mathbf{m}_{t}(j)\;.

Appendix C Number of expected transitions

We can analytically derive the expected number of transitions, i.e., number of transitions where 𝐱s≠𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{s}\neq\mathbf{x}_{t}. First, we recall the update probability:

pλ(𝐱s=j∣𝐱t=i,𝐱)=(1−λ)γs|t𝟏[i=j]+λ(1−γs)𝐪1(j)+wflip𝟏[j=𝐱].\displaystyle p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{s}=j\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=i,\mathbf{x})=(1-\lambda)\gamma_{s\mid t}\mathbf{1}[i=j]+\lambda(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}(j)+w_{\mathrm{flip}}\mathbf{1}[j=\mathbf{x}]. (41)

A transition occurs when j≠ij\neq i. We define the indicator variable C=𝟏[𝐱t≠𝐱s]C=\mathbf{1}[\mathbf{x}_{t}\neq\mathbf{x}_{s}]. Now we want to derive the probability of a transition:

pλ​(C=1∣𝐱t=i,𝐱)=1−pλ​(𝐱s=i∣𝐱t=i,𝐱).\displaystyle p_{\lambda}(C=1\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=i,\mathbf{x})=1-p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{s}=i\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=i,\mathbf{x}). (42)

Next, we condition the probability pλ​(𝐱s=j∣𝐱t=i,𝐱)p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{s}=j\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=i,\mathbf{x}) on two events:

Case 1: 𝐱t≠𝐱\mathbf{x}_{t}\neq\mathbf{x}

In this case, the last term drops out out and the transition simplifies further:

pλ​(𝐱s=𝐱t∣𝐱t≠𝐱)\displaystyle p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{s}=\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}\neq\mathbf{x}) =(1−λ)​γs|t+λ⁡(1−γs)​𝐪1​(𝐱t),\displaystyle=(1-\lambda)\gamma_{s\mid t}+\lambda(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{t}), (43)

and therefore:

pλ​(C=1∣𝐱t≠𝐱)\displaystyle p_{\lambda}(C=1\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}\neq\mathbf{x}) =1−(1−λ)​γs|t−λ⁡(1−γs)​𝐪1​(𝐱t),\displaystyle=1-(1-\lambda)\gamma_{s\mid t}-\lambda(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{t}), (45)
=1−γs|t+λ​γs|t−λ⁡(1−γs)​𝐪1​(𝐱t)\displaystyle=1-\gamma_{s\mid t}+\lambda\gamma_{s\mid t}-\lambda(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) (46)
=A+λ⁡(1−γs1−γt−(1−γs)​𝐪1​(𝐱t))\displaystyle=A+\lambda\left(\frac{1-\gamma_{s}}{1-\gamma_{t}}-(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\right) (47)
=A⏟≥0+λ​((1−γs)​(11−γt−𝐪1​(𝐱t)))⏟≥0\displaystyle=\underbrace{A}_{\geq 0}+\lambda\underbrace{\left((1-\gamma_{s})\left(\frac{1}{1-\gamma_{t}}-\mathbf{q}_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\right)\right)}_{\geq 0} (48)
Case 2: 𝐱t=𝐱\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{x}

Here, we plug in the value of wflipw_{\mathrm{flip}}:

pλ​(𝐱s=𝐱t∣𝐱t=𝐱)\displaystyle p_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}_{s}=\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{x}) =(1−λ)​γs|t+λ⁡(1−γs)​𝐪1​(𝐱)+(1−λ)​(1−γs|t)+λ​γs\displaystyle=(1-\lambda)\gamma_{s\mid t}+\lambda(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}(\mathbf{x})+(1-\lambda)\,(1-\gamma_{s\mid t})+\lambda\,\gamma_{s} (49)

And therefore:

pλ​(C=1∣𝐱t=𝐱)\displaystyle p_{\lambda}(C=1\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{x}) =1−(1−λ)​γs|t−λ⁡(1−γs)​𝐪1​(𝐱)−(1−λ)​(1−γs|t)−λ​γs\displaystyle=1-(1-\lambda)\gamma_{s\mid t}-\lambda(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}(\mathbf{x})-(1-\lambda)\,(1-\gamma_{s\mid t})-\lambda\,\gamma_{s} (50)
=1−(1−λ)−λ⁡(1−γs)​𝐪1​(𝐱)−λ​γs\displaystyle=1-(1-\lambda)-\lambda(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}(\mathbf{x})-\lambda\,\gamma_{s} (51)
=λ−λ⁡(1−γs)​𝐪1​(𝐱)−λ​γs\displaystyle=\lambda-\lambda(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}(\mathbf{x})-\lambda\,\gamma_{s} (52)
=λ⁡(1−(1−γs)​𝐪1​(𝐱)−γs)\displaystyle=\lambda\left(1-(1-\gamma_{s})\mathbf{q}_{1}(\mathbf{x})-\gamma_{s}\right) (53)
=λ​((1−γs)​(1−𝐪1​(𝐱))CLOSE⏟≥0\displaystyle=\lambda\underbrace{\left((1-\gamma_{s})(1-\mathbf{q}_{1}(\mathbf{x})\right)}_{\geq 0} (54)

Finally, we write down the number of total expected transitions:

𝔼⁡[∑t=1TCt]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}C_{t}\right] =∑t=1T𝔼⁡[Ct]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[C_{t}\right] (56)
=∑t=1T𝔼⁡[Ct∣𝐱t=𝐱]​p​(𝐱t=𝐱)+𝔼⁡[Ct∣𝐱t≠𝐱]​p​(𝐱t≠𝐱)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[C_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{x}\right]p(\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{x})+\mathbb{E}\left[C_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}\neq\mathbf{x}\right]p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\neq\mathbf{x}) (57)
=∑i=1Tpλ​(Ct=1∣𝐱t=𝐱)​p​(𝐱t=𝐱)+pλ​(Ct=1∣𝐱t≠𝐱)​p​(𝐱t≠𝐱),\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{T}p_{\lambda}(C_{t}=1\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{x})+p_{\lambda}(C_{t}=1\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}\neq\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\neq\mathbf{x}), (58)

which is a mixture of two functions that are linear with respect to λ\lambda. As the mixture parameters are independent of λ\lambda, the total expected value is linear.

Appendix D Experimental Details

For all experiments we use a linear scheduler for γt\gamma_{t}, i.e., γt=1−t\gamma_{t}=1-t. In the following, we describe dataset specific details.

D.1 Datasets

D.1.1 Text Datasets

We summarize the details of the text dataset in Table 5.

LM1B.

We download the dataset from Hugging Face Datasets (LM1B), and use the bert-base-uncased tokenizer. We pad the sequences to a maximum length of 128. We use the official training, validation, and test splits provided in the dataset.

OpenWebText.

We tokenize using the GPT-2 tokenizer and wrap the sequences to a maximum length of 1024. We adopt the same train-validation splits from Sahoo et al. (2024), where the last 100,000 samples are used for validation.

D.1.2 Molecule datasets

QM9.

The QM9 dataset (Wu et al., 2018) consists of molecules with up to 9 heavy atoms. We use the same split established by (Vignac et al., 2022), and 10000 graphs for evaluation.

GuacaMol.

Furthermore, we evaluate our model on the GuacaMol dataset (Brown et al., 2019). The molecules range from 2 to 88 heavy atoms.

MOSES.

Finally, we benchmark our model on the MOSES dataset (Polykovskiy et al., 2020), spanning filtered molecules from 8 to 27 heavy atoms.

D.2 Model architectures

Text datasets.

For LM1B and OWT training, we use the modified Transformer (Peebles & Xie, 2023) architecture from Sahoo et al. (2024). The model consists of 12 layers, a hidden dimension of 768, and 12 attention heads.

Graph datasets.

For the graph datasets, we use the graph transformer proposed by (Vignac et al., 2022) with the hyperparameters used by (Qin et al., 2024) and Relative Random Walk Probabilities (Ma et al., 2023) as node and edge features. We show our hyperparameters in Table 7.

D.3 Training settings

In Table 7 and Table 8, we report the training hyperparameters used in our experiments for the different datasets.

D.4 Evaluation metrics

D.4.1 Text Generation

Perplexity.

Perplexity is computed as the exponential of the negative average token-level log-likelihood over the evaluation data. We report the perplexities on the test splits following Sahoo et al. (2024).

Generative perplexity.

We report generative perplexity for unconditionally generated sequences, following (Sahoo et al., 2025). We measure it using GPT-2 large (Radford et al., 2019). We further report sample entropy to assess diversity.

D.4.2 Graph Generation

We evaluate the graph generation with standard molecule metrics. We report the validity, uniqueness, i.e., proportion of generated molecules with different SMILES string, and novelty, i.e., proportion of generated molecules not in the training set. Furthermore, we report the Frechet ChemNetDistance (FCD) (Preuer et al., 2018), which measures the embedding similarity of the generated molecules with respect to the training set. Finally, we report the Scaffold similarity and SNN.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
